title: Beyond Orbital Rotations: Correlation-Rank Limits and Clifford-Accessible Measurement, from Algebra and Global Optimization
abstract: Algebra and RANGE global optimization play complementary, explicitly separated roles in identifying measurement structure beyond orbital rotations. In the fixed (1,1)-particle sector of two spatial orbitals per spin, algebra proves that one particle-number-preserving orbital-rotation context contributes a rank-one two-body correlation block $T$: an observable needs at least $\mathrm{rank}\,T$ such contexts, and its best $K$-context correlation-block approximation is exactly the Eckart-Young singular-value tail, attained by the truncated SVD. A continuous RANGE search over the physical rotation angles independently corroborates this exact trade-off. A Bell-diagonal, Heisenberg-type witness has correlation rank three: it needs at least three orbital-rotation contexts, while one explicit physical Clifford circuit measures its commuting Pauli representatives. For spin-conserving Jordan-Wigner molecular Hamiltonians we also prove the parity ceiling $r_X \le 2(N-1)$ for any Pauli subset, tight even within commuting subsets; $X$-rank is a routing diagnostic, and the strict separation is carried by the correlation-rank theorem. The discrete mode of RANGE locates high-$X$-rank commuting families across molecular and production f-element Hamiltonians, finding ceiling-saturating witnesses for CH4 and NdO; values are best found unless a proved ceiling is attained. Applying the companion certificate framework, enlarging product settings by fully commuting, Clifford-accessible settings reduces the certified leading shot cost by 31-70% on four 29-35-qubit f-element Hamiltonians, a QWC-versus-QWC+FC result rather than a Gaussian-versus-Clifford pricing. Controlled-Pauli insertions in Hadamard tests are Clifford; these zero-$T$ statements concern measurement circuitry only, while shot counts and state preparation retain their full costs.
summary: This work rigorously compares two ways to measure quantum observables: physically motivated 'orbital rotations' versus those achievable with Clifford gates. Using algebraic bounds and optimization techniques on fermionic Hamiltonians, the authors prove that leveraging Clifford-accessible measurement contexts offers substantial resource savings (up to 70%) over purely orbital-rotation methods for large molecular systems.
main_problem: The paper compares the measurement resource requirements for quantum observables, contrasting those achievable via physical 'orbital rotations' against those accessible using purely Clifford-circuit measurements.
main_result: Clifford-accessible measurement contexts provide a significant computational advantage, reducing the certified leading shot cost by 31–70% compared to orbital-rotation contexts when applied to large f-element Hamiltonians.
method: The authors use algebraic proofs (correlation rank) and global optimization searches (RANGE) to establish rigorous lower bounds on measurement context complexity and compare resource costs.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on fermionic Hamiltonians mapped onto Pauli operators, specifically examining the fixed (1,1)-particle sector with two spatial orbitals per spin, often involving heavy-element systems like NdO or CeO.
key_observables: Correlation Rank, X-rank ($r_X$), and measurement shot cost $M(\epsilon)$ are key diagnostics used to quantify context complexity and resource requirements.
important_parameters: The parity ceiling $r_X \le 2(N-1)$ is a crucial theoretical bound derived for spin-conserving Hamiltonians; the reduction factor (31–70%) quantifies the practical advantage of Clifford circuits.
main_assumptions: The resource conclusion is limited to basis changes and controlled-Pauli insertions being Clifford; sampling, state preparation, and noise costs are assumed to retain their full cost structure.
figures_summary: Tables summarize empirical results for various molecules (e.g., CH4) showing high X-rank values approaching theoretical ceilings, and another table compares the resource savings on f-element Hamiltonians when using Clifford vs. orbital rotation contexts.
paper_structure: The paper builds from algebraic proofs establishing context obstructions (correlation rank), to continuous optimization corroboration (RANGE), and culminates in applying these findings to estimate practical measurement costs for complex molecular/f-element systems, showing the superiority of Clifford methods.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for determining the minimal quantum resources needed to simulate complex electronic structure problems, directly impacting the feasibility assessment of quantum chemistry algorithms.
